title: Markets and moods: bull, bear, correction, timing, compounding
objectives: Explain bull, bear and correction falls, and why timing is hard.
Say how rupee cost averaging and time in the market help a SIP investor.
body_md:
A bull market is a long period of rising prices; a bear market is a fall of about 20% or more from the peak, often lasting months; a correction is a fall of about 10–20% from a recent peak and happens most years. Market timing — buying at lows and selling at highs — is very hard to do consistently, and waiting for “the right time” often means staying out too long. Time in the market matters more: missing a few of the best days can cut long-term returns sharply. A fixed SIP buys more units when prices are low and fewer when high, so the average cost evens out.

| Term | Plain meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bull market | A long period of rising prices and optimism | Everyone talks about stocks at dinner |
| Bear market | A fall of about 20% or more from the peak, often lasting months | March 2020 crash |
| Correction | A fall of about 10–20% from a recent peak; normal and frequent | Happens most years in equity markets |
| Market timing | Trying to buy at lows and sell at highs; very hard to do consistently | Waiting for "the right time" often means staying out too long |
| Time in the market | Staying invested long enough for compounding to work | Missing a few of the best days can cut long-term returns sharply |
| Rupee cost averaging | A fixed SIP buys more units when prices are low and fewer when high, so the average cost evens out | ₹10,000 buys 200 units at ₹50, 250 units at ₹40 |

> **Talk-track:** “Markets fall regularly; that's the price of equity returns. A SIP actually buys more units when prices are down. The real question is whether your goal date has changed, not whether the market has.”
example: ₹10,000 buys 200 units at NAV ₹50 and 250 units at ₹40 — falls help a SIP investor who keeps going.
say: A correction is normal; it happens most years.
A SIP buys more units when prices are low.
never: Waiting for the perfect day to invest is a reliable strategy.
A 10% fall means the market is finished.
